To outshine someone or something means to be so much better, more impressive, or more brilliant that the other person or thing looks dull or less significant by comparison.

Think of it this way: when the sun rises, the stars don't disappear — but they seem to disappear, because the sun's light is so powerful it drowns out their glow completely. That relationship — where one thing is so bright it makes everything else fade — is the heart of what "outshine" means.

This verb works on two levels, and both are correct and common:

1. The Literal Meaning (about actual light)

When one source of light is so much brighter than another that the other one can barely be noticed.

"The stadium floodlights outshine every streetlamp around it."

Here, you are talking about real, physical brightness.

2. The Figurative Meaning (about people, talent, and performance)

This is by far the more common and important use. When a person — through their talent, skill, beauty, intelligence, charm, or achievement — performs so impressively that others around them look ordinary or lesser in comparison, that person outshines the others.

"At the school talent show, Maya outshone every other performer with her singing."

Maya didn't make the others disappear. They were still there, still performing. But Maya was so good that, in comparison, the others seemed much less impressive.
The Hidden Logic of the Word

Here is something important to understand: outshining is always relative. You cannot outshine in isolation. You always outshine something or someone. The word only makes sense when there is a comparison happening.

Also — and this is subtle but important — the person being outshone is not necessarily bad or weak. They might be very good. But the person outshining them is simply better, or more noticeable, in that particular moment or context.

"The veteran actors were talented, but the young newcomer outshone them all at the awards ceremony."

The veterans are still talented. The newcomer just shone brighter.

The word carries a sense of effortless superiority — it feels less aggressive than words like "defeat" or "crush," but it still implies a clear winner and a clear loser in terms of impressiveness. It is often used to describe someone who naturally stands out rather than someone who fights to win.

It can sometimes carry a slightly uncomfortable undertone — being outshone can feel like being overshadowed or upstaged, which is not always a pleasant experience for the person on the receiving end.
Common Contexts Where You'll See It

• Performance & talent: "Her debut novel outshone everything else published that year."
  • Beauty & appearance: "The bride was stunning, but her maid of honor somehow outshone her in the photos."
  • Academic or professional achievement: "He outshone his colleagues by delivering results no one else could match."
  • Products & technology: "The new phone outshines its competitors in battery life and camera quality."
All the Verb Forms You'll Need

FormExample
Base"She will outshine everyone."
Third person (he/she/it)"He outshines all his rivals."
Past tense"She outshone everyone at the gala." (Note: not "outshined" — though "outshined" is sometimes seen, outshone is the standard and preferred past form.)
Present participle"She is outshining the competition."
Past participle"He has outshone every predecessor."

To outshine means to be so much more impressive, brilliant, or capable than others — in any quality, from literal brightness to talent to beauty — that by comparison, those others seem dim or ordinary.
